title: Speeding up Energy System Models - a Best Practice Guide
contribution: A 22-author BEAM-ME guide that benchmarks aggregation and heuristic temporal decomposition on the 488-node, 8,760-hour REMix LP (DLR chapters) and documents PIPS-IPM++, PIPS-IPM extended to arrowhead LPs with linking constraints through locality-aware Schur complements, a distributed preconditioner, interior-point changes, parallel scaling and structure-preserving presolve, together with GAMS model annotation, solving energy-system LPs of up to 1.15 billion variables that commercial solvers could not (pp. 42, 68, 71-75, 85-93, 103-105).
problem_entry: Application wall: GAMS energy-system LPs at weeks-to-a-month run times and 100 GB or more on single servers, beyond CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress and SCIP and only trivially parallelizable (p. 13); commercial solvers cannot run distributed (pp. 71, 104) and the open-source PIPS-IPM lacks linking constraints (p. 72); extending it was chosen after a survey of open-source HPC solvers (p. 14).
key_idea: Keep PIPS-IPM's MPI distribution and Schur-complement decomposition, add linking constraints, use that most linking rows and columns couple only two blocks to keep the Schur complement sparse, or solve it by a Krylov method with a distributed preconditioner; add Gondzio's correctors, separate primal and dual step lengths, parallel geometric scaling and presolve that keeps the block structure (pp. 71-75).
assumptions: Continuous LPs only (p. 73) with block-diagonal structure plus linking variables and linking constraints, supplied by modeller annotation in GAMS rather than detected (eq. 4.1, pp. 71, 85-86); locality of linking (p. 73); time blocks preferred to regions (pp. 98, 118); test models REMix, ELMOD, YSSP, SIMPLE and six partner models (pp. 20, 39-42, 104-105, 139); correctness rests only on the equivalence of scaled and presolved LPs to the original (p. 74).
proof_devices: Schur-complement elimination of the block-bordered interior-point system, steps 1-4 with C = K_0 - sum of B_i^T K_i^-1 B_i (eq. 4.3, p. 73)
nonzero pattern of the Schur complement predicted from the locality of linking constraints and variables, enabling sparse storage and sparse solves (p. 73)
Krylov solve with a distributed preconditioner instead of an explicit Schur complement (p. 73); measured 415 s to 203 s on ELMOD CWE15 (p. 110)
scaling equivalence A~ = RAC with positive diagonal R and C, solutions mapped back by x = C x~ at equal objective (eqs. 4.4-4.5, p. 74)
structure-preserving presolve invariant: four equivalence reductions undone by postsolve, none may alter the block structure (p. 74)
experiments: JUWELS: strong scaling on one SIMPLE instance (5.6 M variables, 512 blocks, process counts dividing the blocks, 2 OpenMP threads per MPI process) with a reduced PIPS-IPM++ as ablation (pp. 103-104); Table 5.1, eight instances up to 1.15 B variables on 19-128 nodes against the best of CPLEX 12.8, Gurobi 8.1, MOSEK 8.1 and Xpress 8.4.7 at 16 threads, I/O included, OOM kept: 181 and 216 s against 6,201 and 6,111 s, the rest OOM (pp. 104-105); single runs, no seeds; Scalasca and Vampir trace, 415 s to 203 s (pp. 106-110); DLR chapter: CPLEX deterministic ticks, mismatches printed, Table 3.5 (pp. 48, 65-66, 68).
positioning: Extends PIPS-IPM (Petra, Schenk, Anitescu 2014; p. 72); Cook's TSP as the precedent for hand-tailored solvers (p. 71); components credited to Colombo and Gondzio, Wright, Elble and Sahinidis, Achterberg et al., Andersen and Andersen, Gondzio, Vanderbei (pp. 73-75); commercial solvers as the bar, not criticized (pp. 103-104); the DLR chapters set exact decomposition aside (pp. 38, 66).
writing: Practitioner guide with hedged imperatives and labelled rules of thumb (p. 17), mathematics deferred to ZIB reports (pp. 72-74), command-level examples (pp. 86-101); headline factors do not reconcile (26 in Ch. 7, 34 and 28 computed from Table 5.1, 50-70 in §6.3; pp. 105, 118, 124); uncounted 'some models' (pp. 117-118); draft traces (pp. 14, 66, 118).
limits_future: PIPS-IPM++ fails on some strongly linked or badly scaled partner models (pp. 117-118); finding a good annotation is not automated (p. 118); model generation is the bottleneck, with a 2,147,483,647-nonzero cap (p. 90); results withheld (pp. 105, 117); future: more presolve, more aggressive scaling, homogeneous self-dual method, hierarchical Schur complement (pp. 74-75), generic distributed model generation (p. 90).

method_links.note: Group and consortium level: the prototype lost to CPLEX's interior-point code and failed on some ESMs, and the guide lists the changes that followed (pp. 72-74); §4.1.3 prints the next components (pp. 74-75), which later works take up by title (S068 2020, S027 2022, S078 2026; not read here). Weaker than his counted ledger: the model-experiment failures are uncounted (pp. 117-118).

Baselines given, not constructed: per-instance best of four commercial solvers at their best thread count, an ablated PIPS-IPM++ with only the Schur-complement decomposition, and a nodes-times-time argument for the hardware mismatch (pp. 72, 103-105); the DLR chapter prints its hardware and precision mismatches as step 5 asks (pp. 65-66). Counter-example in the co-signed text: Chapter 7's 'up to a factor of 26' without baseline or subset (p. 124).

The scaling instance is chosen by stated criteria (solvable by one process, 512 blocks for a power-of-2 plot, process counts dividing the blocks) from the synthetic SIMPLE family with a documented deterministic data generator: an instrument for prototyping and scaling, not a library with admission rules or public corrections; appendix authors not stated.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: PIPS-IPM++ presolve admits only equivalence reductions with postsolve that keep the block structure the parallel interior-point method exploits; the line continues in S068 (2020) and S078 (2026) by title. Group evidence; ZIB authorship of §4.1 inferred.

A distributed solver on 19 nodes is compared with the best single-node commercial solver by wall clock (181 against 6,201 s) and by run time per computing resource, with I/O included and OOM kept as an outcome. ZIB authorship of §5.1 inferred.

transferable: Presolve for a structure-exploiting solver: admit only reductions that keep the block structure, run a cheap cleanup (redundant rows, negligibly small entries) first, keep every reduction reversible by postsolve (p. 74); carrying it to presolve before a MILP decomposition is an inference.
Predict the Schur complement's sparsity from the locality of linking constraints and variables and factor it sparsely; switch to a preconditioned Krylov solve when linkage is strong (p. 73).

Against shared-memory solvers, give each commercial solver its best thread count, take the per-instance best, include I/O, keep OOM as a result, and add a nodes-times-seconds comparison to the wall-clock factor (pp. 104-105).
Put an ablated version of the new solver (core decomposition only) into the scaling plot to show what the added algorithms buy (p. 103).
For a strong-scaling study pick an instance one process solves in reasonable time, with 2^k blocks and process counts that divide the block count (p. 103).

Find the parallel bottleneck with trace tools (instrumentation with a filter, wait states, delay costs, critical path, before-and-after timelines) before tuning; here one serial factorization on rank 0 (pp. 106-111).
Without exclusive identical machines, use the solver's deterministic ticks as the time measure and print each remaining mismatch with its likely effect (pp. 48, 65-66).

Measure numerics hygiene per instance size: slack and penalty costs in the range of real costs (coefficient range ideally below 1e5), explicit bounds, input rounding; effects can invert with size (pp. 50-52).
coauthors: Yvonne Scholz, Benjamin Fuchs, Frieder Borggrefe, Karl-Kien Cao, Manuel Wetzel, Kai von Krbek, Felix Cebulla, Hans Christian Gils (DLR); Frederik Fiand, Michael Bussieck (GAMS); Thorsten Koch (TU Berlin); Daniel Rehfeldt (ZIB); Dmitry Khabi (HLRS); Thomas Breuer, Daniel Rohe (Juelich); Hannes Hobbie, David Schönheit (TU Dresden); Hasan Ümitcan Yilmaz (KIT); Evangelos Panos (PSI); Samir Jeddi (Cologne); Stefanie Buchholz (DTU) (p. 1). No section bylines; chapters 1-3 based on Cao et al. 2019 (DLR; pp. 13, 27, 37); §4.1 and §5.1 inferred to be the ZIB group's (Rehfeldt, Gleixner, Koch; pp. 73-74, 104).
